entries.knowledge: The non-desklamp search step was progressively rewritten from a family-level single-pass sweep into a stronger per-candidate sweep. The current diff adds: treat each individual closed container (cabinet, drawer, fridge, microwave, safe) and each open surface as a separate candidate rather than ending a family after one or two empty members; after arriving at an already-open empty receptacle, or one whose visible contents match an already inspected location, do not open, re-examine, or linger, but leave for an uninspected candidate; and if the same small set of locations keeps reappearing without yielding the target, stop revisiting them while the step budget allows. Current paired evidence is mixed, and the search change was applied jointly with a temperature clause. In a two-book-to-desk task, the Parent reached the 50-step limit while cycling among desk, shelves, and drawers; the Candidate eventually went to bed 1 (an open surface), took one book, placed it, returned to bed for the second book, and succeeded in 40 steps. However, the Candidate also returned repeatedly to already-open empty drawers, shelves, and the desk before reaching bed, so the stop-revisiting part of the wording was not reliably followed. In a heat-apple-to-diningtable task where the exact apple was not located, both Parent and Candidate hit the 50-step limit, and the Candidate continued cycling among the fridge, countertops, and cabinets without reaching a diningtable; the new wording therefore did not prevent step-limit cycling when the target was not discovered. Other current pairs preserved success: the Candidate added an early empty-cabinet check in the cool-plate pair and finished one step later than the Parent, and in the two-creditcard pair it went directly to the desk and completed in 9 steps versus the Parent's 24 after many drawer checks, though no search-order rule fixes that starting choice. Earlier single-pass-sweep evidence likewise included rescues when the exact target lay in an uninspected family, but also step-limit cycling when the target was absent or not found. The supported pattern is that the expanded per-candidate and anti-loop wording can accompany a rescue when the exact target exists in an otherwise uninspected open surface or container, but it does not ensure consistent non-revisiting or success when the target is absent or not discovered within budget.

Across successive non-desklamp general-procedure edits, temperature guidance now tells the Actor, after acquiring the exact target, to go to the appropriate appliance and perform the explicit cool-X-with-fridge or heat-X-with-microwave action directly on the held target as soon as that action is admissible, even before opening the appliance; open the appliance only when needed, treat one heat or cool action as sufficient, avoid extra close/open cycles or moving the target into and out of the appliance, and then go directly to the requested destination. Earlier paired evidence already showed that once the exact target was acquired, the Candidate applied the temperature action while holding it and avoided Parent-style insert/close/reopen cycles, with large savings and success in cool-pot (11 vs 18 steps), hot-apple (9 vs 35), heat-egg (15 vs 40), hot-potato (7 vs 14), and heat-tomato (7 vs 21) tasks; when the exact target could not be located, as in heat-plate and hot-mug tasks, the guidance had no opportunity and did not prevent step-limit failure. The current pairs repeat the pattern when the exact target was found: in cool-plate-to-countertop, the Parent opened the fridge before cooling while the Candidate cooled the plate at the closed fridge, although an extra cabinet check made the Candidate finish in 9 rather than 8 steps; in cool-tomato-to-microwave, the Candidate cooled the tomato at the fridge and finished in 10 versus the Parent's 18; in heat-tomato-to-fridge, the Candidate heated the tomato while holding it at the closed microwave with one action and finished in 8 steps, while the Parent inserted it and repeatedly closed and opened the microwave before heating it, taking 39; and in another heat-tomato-to-fridge pair the Candidate heated at the closed microwave in 7 steps versus the Parent's 8 after opening the microwave. In a heat-apple-to-diningtable task where no exact apple was found, both hit the step limit, so the temperature clause did not help target discovery. The evidence therefore supports a robust local reduction in appliance manipulation and step use conditional on acquiring the exact target, including direct action at a closed appliance; it does not guarantee task success when the target is not found, and the current temperature change was applied jointly with a search change, so whole-task step differences are not solely attributable to it.
